approach.method_basis: The Parent trains a recurrent SMILES model on original unlabeled molecular strings and publishes the single checkpoint with the best ordinary heldout token loss. An objective starts an adaptable copy and retains the published model as a frozen reference. Accepted neural samples refresh a graph-breeding population and provide a protected parent at the first graph handoff; a fingerprint posterior using accepted scores selects the other offspring. Graph observations then train the neural policy through trajectory balance and the learned normalizer. That complete reciprocal method is retained. Only the estimate of reusable neural weights produced by unlabeled preparation changes.
approach.novelty: Track an exponential moving average of the unlabeled training weights and let ordinary heldout token loss select among those averaged checkpoints. The average combines nearby stages of the same training trajectory, rather than publishing one instantaneous state. This differs from the tested alternative-string augmentation and molecular-yield checkpoint ranking, and from changing the frequency of training examples. Original data, gradient updates and online adaptation stay fixed, while a final unlabeled comparison measures what the averaged and ordinary minimum-loss priors emit.

hypothesis: Publish a validation-selected exponential moving average of unlabeled recurrent training weights, with decay 0.999 and the Parent raw training trajectory and raw-NLL stopping rule preserved.

finding_summary.headline: Averaged priors improved holdout loss and pure-prior yield, with a small, uneven score gain.
finding_summary.insights:
This provides evidence that averaging the same unlabeled weight trajectory can produce a better reusable prior without changing training examples, gradient updates or the online algorithm. Exact raw checkpoint identities and matching raw loss histories rule out altered raw training as the explanation. The final pure-prior comparison was excluded from checkpoint selection, so its consistent yield improvement adds evidence beyond the heldout criterion that selected the average. The early lag also limits the result: the benefit appears after substantial training, and is not evidence that averaged weights are preferable throughout learning.

Better pure-prior likelihood and parseable yield were insufficient to improve validity after task adaptation or provide broad task gains. The chemistry explains why the score increase deserves a narrower interpretation: ordinary aryl/carbonyl and amine families coexist with N-fluorinated motifs, unusual hydrogen-bearing sulfur, azide/acyl-halide assemblies and contracted rings. Favorable scores do not establish those connections as necessary or synthetically credible. Explicit stereochemical configurations remain absent. The remaining question is how much of the improved reusable prior can survive accepted-score adaptation while retaining credible functional-group attachment and useful core coverage; this experiment demonstrates the averaging effect, but does not resolve that downstream limitation.
finding_summary.results:
The averaged weights were distinct from the raw weights throughout validation, and all 6,633 logged coordinate updates matched the registered recurrence. The raw training losses and final raw checkpoint identities remained exactly equal to the Parent. All three preparations completed 29,742 updates and selected the final averaged state by ordinary holdout loss. Mean selected token loss fell from 0.564577 to 0.559834, improving in every seed. Averaging initially lagged the raw model, but its loss stayed lower at every validation from step 5,000 onward in all three seeds.

The final unscored diagnostic also improved in every seed. Across three 4,096-sample panels per model, valid terminated yield increased from 90.41% to 91.85%, giving 177 more valid strings. Each individual panel had no canonical duplicates or missing EOS, so its valid and canonical-unique yields were equal. The gains were 2.34, 1.54 and 0.44 percentage points across seeds. This pure-prior gain did not carry through to higher adapted-policy validity: across the same 12,000 online draws, validity was 70.06% versus Parent 70.34%, with first-batch validity 90.92% versus 91.17% and later-batch validity 67.74% versus 68.03%.

All fifteen tasks completed. Three-seed mean final Top-1 rose from 0.520669 to 0.527370; paired gains were 0.000602, 0.004046 and 0.015453. The improvement was concentrated in sitagliptin, while deco-hop and median scores fell in every seed and zaleplon was mixed. Recorded mean preparation time was 238.0 seconds versus 259.5 seconds, with identical training horizons; these total timings do not isolate the extra averaging and diagnostic cost.

molecular.headline: Aryl carbonyl and amine families coexist with azide/acyl-halide assemblies, N-fluorinated rings and unusual hydrogen-bearing sulfur.
molecular.overall_character: All 4,500 child and 4,500 Parent trajectory rows were read. Each node supplies 900 observations per task, including 870 optimizer proposals, for 4,350 proposals overall. Every emitted child SMILES parses with the supplied RDKit environment. The output contains ordinary aryl ketones and amides, aza-aromatics, arylpiperazines and oxygen-containing rings, but also contracted unsaturated rings, complex nitrogen/carbonyl assemblies, hydrazones, azides, acyl halides and N-fluorinated structures. The digest ring-closure rates are 0.9759–0.9920 and aromatic-marker rates 0.9241–0.9770; these measure presence in SMILES text rather than aromatic atom fraction or geometric plausibility. Read-only RDKit median heavy-atom counts are 25, 36, 30, 33 and 26 in the supplied task order, with median ring counts of three, four, four, five and three. Chemical plausibility is mixed: several leading families have conventional ingredients, while other high examples contain sensitive bonding and unusual valence or ring topology. Each task has stereocentre_rate 0.0; unassigned stereogenic centres occur in 325, 312, 540, 519 and 367 optimizer proposals respectively, and assigned centres in none. Different seeds reach different families, but their high neighborhoods often concentrate on related decorations or ring edits. These observations describe the chemistry and its limitations without judging mechanism activation or node eligibility.

per_task.generated_character: The leading seed-2 family joins a hydroxyquinazoline-like bicyclic aza-aromatic group to an ortho-methylphenyl carbonyl group through a short substituted linker. The leader is a ketone with a methyl-bearing stereogenic carbon; it has 24 heavy atoms and three aromatic six-membered rings. A close family contains the corresponding tertiary benzamide connection. Other high molecules use a diaryl ether with sulfinamide or thioamide linkage, and seed 0 explores aryl thioethers/carboxylic acids connected to thiazole-like or contracted four-membered unsaturated nitrogen rings. Much of this is recognizable carbonyl and heteroaromatic chemistry, although the short unsaturated ring and some sulfur attachments are less straightforward. The child and Parent both have median 25 heavy atoms and three rings. Parent leaders included biaryl pyrazole/acetanilide and quinoline/urea arrangements, so the change is in useful attachment patterns rather than a general new ability to make aromatic or carbonyl groups.
liabilities: A high seed-0 example contains a four-membered unsaturated nitrogen ring. Its valence-valid graph does not establish low strain or synthetic accessibility.
Sulfinamide, thioamide, sulfonamide and thioether attachments have different electronic and reactive behavior; the score does not make them interchangeable or establish their stability.
Tiny fragments and much larger linked structures occur in the low tail, while the useful examples are moderate in size. Their substituted and bridged centres are not stereochemically specified.
missing_features: Chemically distinct compact cores preserving the useful carbonyl, aza-aromatic and linker relationships are not consistently established among the high neighbors; many modifications instead alter several local relationships at once.
Defined configurations of the leading methyl-bearing ketone and of stereogenic sulfur or saturated-ring variants are absent. The observations do not establish a preferred configuration.
The high carbonyl families do not identify a uniquely required absent functional group; both ketone and amide connections are already represented.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The methyl-substituted ketone scores 0.4597940970593737, the unfluorinated tertiary amide 0.458386638264238, and its fluorinated analogue 0.4425635194548914. Adding a phenol in either of two cited positions gives 0.44813028323800735. These close families associate high values with a particular short carbonyl/linker/aza-aromatic arrangement; they do not support indiscriminate fluorination or hydroxylation. The four-membered unsaturated nitrogen-ring example scores 0.4458257099418776, while a related thiazole-like structure scores 0.4340282562885518. Sulfinamide and thioamide diaryl ethers both reach 0.4443186615775074. A late sulfonamide diaryl ether scores 0.17956483181835844, but its other structural changes prevent assigning that difference solely to sulfur oxidation state. Acetylene and NCl score 0.0, and a large bridged/polyfunctional assembly scores 1.444798552479113e-61. The digest median is 0.137716.

per_task.generated_character: The leading seed-1 family is an amino/chloro-substituted heteroaryl hydrazone attached to a fused aza-aromatic carbonyl framework. The leader has 25 heavy atoms and perceived ring sizes of six, four and six: the carbonyl/hydrazone portion lies in an unusually small fused four-membered ring. Another high family is a larger, heavily aminated heteroaromatic assembly with sulfur/nitrogen substituents. Seed 2 instead produces large azide-bearing heteroaromatic and polyunsaturated assemblies, often containing acyl chloride functionality. The child median is 36 heavy atoms and four rings, as in the Parent, but 191 of 870 proposals exceed 50 heavy atoms versus 128 Parent proposals. The maximum is 103 heavy atoms. Parent chemistry already included hydrazones and aminoheteroaromatics; the new output changes their core geometry and develops a conspicuous azide/acyl-halide tail. The digest cumulated-double-bond marker rate is 0.1322, but this should not be read as an allene fraction: graph inspection finds 103 azide-bearing proposals and only four with a C=C=C substructure.
liabilities: The upper hydrazone family uses a fused four-membered carbonyl-containing ring, with strain and synthetic-persistence questions not resolved by graph parsing.

Azide substructures occur in 103 of 870 child proposals versus one Parent proposal; acyl halides occur in 46 versus none. The cited late structures combine these motifs with dense unsaturation and linked aromatic systems. These are distinct chemical reactivity flags, not a claim that every isolated azide is intrinsically unmakeable.

Large assemblies, occasional short ring closures and reactive terminal carbonyl groups leave physical-property balance and synthesis unestablished. Unassigned stereogenic centres occur in 312 proposals.
missing_features: Ordinary ring-size and linkage alternatives preserving the favorable heteroaromatic/hydrazone/carbonyl arrangement are not demonstrated as a controlled high-scoring series.

Chemically coherent terminal groups and moderate-sized core replacements are incompletely represented around the azide/acyl-halide assemblies. Their acceptance does not identify azide or acyl-halide chemistry as an objective requirement.
The observations do not establish a uniquely missing target group; the visible deficiencies concern geometry, connection context and practical realization of the useful polar/aromatic arrangement.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The contracted carbonyl/hydrazone leader scores 0.6022255972895614 and the larger aminated heteroaromatic example 0.6015432789085216. Closely related hydrazone variants score 0.5990035358405658, 0.5988330554894022 and 0.5987685190973308 despite changes to nitrogen, fluorine or amino substitution. This narrow upper spread supports a useful heteroaromatic/polar arrangement but does not establish that ring contraction or a particular halogen is necessary. A late large azide/acyl-chloride assembly scores 0.5838410524613145; another elaborated azide structure scores 0.5899213188460097. Such values do not certify those structures as stable products. A sulfone/amide-rich unsaturated low example scores 0.26625106564364875 and a sulfonamide/cyclic-sulfone structure 0.2680563357675949. The digest median is 0.558467. Many familiar polar groups occur in both low and high molecules, so their relative connection is more informative than their count.

per_task.generated_character: The strongest seed-2 molecules are arylpiperazines joined by carbon chains to oxygen-containing benzofused saturated rings. Their aryl partner carries a methylamino or methylaminomethyl group; some linkers also contain an imine. The leader has 28 heavy atoms and four six-membered rings, two aromatic, with one unassigned stereogenic centre in the oxygen-ring system. Related variants change oxygen-ring size, linker length, chlorine placement or aminomethyl substitution. Seed 1 includes aza-aromatic piperazines with a propyl-pyrrolidine arm, while seed 0 also provides linked saturated amines and sulfur/nitrogen aromatics. The Parent already generated arylpiperidines, aminoalkyl linkers and oxygen-containing ring systems. The child median is 30 heavy atoms and four rings versus 28 and four in the Parent. The charged-marker rate is only 0.0103, but neutral secondary and tertiary amines remain plentiful.
liabilities: Long flexible linkers, multiple amines and aromatic regions leave physicochemical balance unmeasured even where the observed score is high.

Some high relatives introduce imines, chloromethyl groups, aminooxy connections or contracted oxygen rings. These changes have distinct chemical consequences that are not resolved by the near-limit scores.
Unassigned stereogenic centres occur in 540 of 870 proposals, with none assigned; the leading oxygen-ring family already contains such centres.
missing_features: No further required pharmacophoric group is identifiable from the near-limit upper tail; accessible amines, aromatic regions and oxygen-ring variants are already present.
Defined configurations and controlled linker/ring geometry are absent for the substituted oxygen-ring and branched amine families. The data do not establish a preferred configuration.
Core and linker changes do not consistently retain the favorable arrangement without multiplying large fragments or altering nitrogen/oxygen attachment context.

per_task.generated_character: The high seed-0 family is a large nitrogen-rich carbonyl assembly with phenyl and ethoxy/ester-substituted aryl groups, connected through a sulfonyl group to a methylene-substituted morpholine-like ring. The leader has 43 heavy atoms and five six-membered rings, only two aromatic. Related structures change cyclic urea/imide connections, introduce N–N or N–S bonds, or fuse additional oxygen-containing rings. Seed 2 also generates large bridged diaryl carbonyl systems with saturated nitrogen rings. These retain the Parent broad carbonyl/polycycle/amine pattern but realize it in different, densely substituted frameworks. The child median is 33 heavy atoms and five rings versus 36 and five in the Parent; the upper example is therefore larger than the middle of its own proposal distribution. Many component groups are familiar, but the combined junctions and heteroatom connections make synthetic plausibility uncertain.
liabilities: Dense cyclic urea/imide-like groups, sulfur/nitrogen connections and exocyclic methylene groups create electronic and reactivity questions that the molecular scores do not answer.

The complex linked and bridged arrangements lack supplied synthetic routes or conformational evidence. Unassigned stereogenic centres occur in 519 proposals, including several centres in some near-high fused variants.

Large duplicated structures and small low-information fragments remain in the tail, although the overall median size is lower than the Parent and 58 proposals exceed 50 heavy atoms versus 74 Parent proposals.
missing_features: Less encumbered, chemically coherent alternative cores preserving useful nitrogen/carbonyl/aromatic relationships are not systematically established; near-equal simpler relatives suggest that full elaboration is not uniformly required.
Configuration and ring-junction geometry are not specified for the saturated, bridged or fused systems, including the leading molecule.
The supplied structures do not identify one uniquely missing target fragment. Their limiting chemistry is the controlled arrangement and practical realization of familiar groups.

per_task.generated_character: The seed-1 leader combines an N-fluorinated diazacycle, an imine-containing nitrogen ring and an unusual hydrogen-bearing sulfur centre. That sulfur has an oxo bond, a hydroxy bond, nitrogen and carbon attachments, and an explicit hydrogen; it is not simply an ordinary sulfone. The leader has 25 heavy atoms and perceived ring sizes of five, five and seven, with no perceived aromatic ring despite the aromatic content elsewhere in the task pool. Related molecules retain N–F in sulfonyl-imine/diazacycle arrangements. Seed 2 instead produces an N-fluorinated fused nitrogen/carbonyl system connected to a halogenated diene and fluoroethyl ester. The Parent high chemistry already included an N-fluorohydrazino azetidine and nitroso/carbonyl nitrogen-ring variants, but the child has 198 N–halogen-bearing proposals versus 22 Parent proposals, and [SH] text in 64 versus one. Thus the unusual nitrogen-fluorine and sulfur representation is much more prominent. The child median is 26 heavy atoms and three rings versus 24 and three in the Parent.

The fused N-fluorinated carbonyl/diene family combines sensitive heteroatom substitution with unsaturation; a late variant introduces an acyl fluoride as well. These are different chemical issues from conventional carbon-bound fluorine.

Expanded or contracted unsaturated rings, large linked assemblies and unspecified stereochemistry complicate interpretation. Unassigned stereogenic centres occur in 367 of 870 proposals, with none assigned.

Defined configurations of the substituted diazacycles and fused carbonyl frameworks are absent. The data do not identify an appropriate stereoisomer.

Controlled changes in core and linker size that retain the narrow favorable polar-group arrangement are incomplete; the observations do not identify a uniquely missing target heterocycle or amine placement.

The upper excerpt therefore retains N–F across quite different arrangements, without establishing that N-fluorination is necessary or chemically stable. Extending the diene-containing linker gives only 8.672801865236684e-07, and a late acyl-fluoride-containing variant scores 0.04566061972684397. Large polar, polyaryl and nitrogen-rich assemblies include exact-zero observations. The digest median is 0.003446. These whole-molecule comparisons support compact and specific polar/halogen/ring arrangements, not a generic more-fluorine or more-nitrogen rule.

transferable_gaps.evidence: The high excerpt includes an N-fluorinated diazacycle with hydrogen-bearing oxo/hydroxy sulfur at 0.4626580698584027 and an N-fluorinated carbonyl/diene system at 0.41805207108748615. Direct N–halogen bonds occur in 198 of 870 proposals in that set versus 22 Parent proposals. Another set contains 103 azide-bearing and 46 acyl-halide-bearing proposals versus one and zero in its Parent, with such groups directly visible in accepted late molecules. Conventional ketone/amide and arylpiperazine families are also present, so the issue is uneven preservation of useful chemistry rather than a universal inability to make ordinary groups.
transferable_gaps.gap: Chemically credible functional-group attachment and valence are not consistently preserved within favorable output families.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Make stable, chemically coherent alternatives available while retaining the surrounding polar and aromatic arrangement. Distinguish carbon-bound fluorine from N-fluorination, ordinary sulfur oxidation states from unusual hydrogen-bearing coordination, and stable carbonyl groups from acyl halides. Treat imine, hydrazone, azide, amine and amide attachments as different chemical environments for accepted feedback to evaluate.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Cited high molecules include a four-membered unsaturated nitrogen ring, a fused four-membered carbonyl/hydrazone ring, varied oxygen-ring sizes and densely bridged nitrogen/carbonyl systems. Every task digest gives stereocentre_rate 0.0. Read-only RDKit checks find unassigned stereogenic centres in 325, 312, 540, 519 and 367 optimizer proposals in the brief task order, with assigned centres in none; examples include the leading methyl-bearing ketone and substituted oxygen-ring amines.
transferable_gaps.gap: Control of ring geometry and explicit stereochemistry is incomplete in the complex structures the generator emits.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Support chemically credible ring closures, expansions and contractions together with explicit configurations for existing stereogenic centres. Keep topology, saturation and stereochemistry changes separable so the current accepted observations can compare defined arrangements. Missing specification alone does not establish a benefit for a chosen configuration.

transferable_gaps.evidence: A late duplicated aromatic/amine assembly scores 0.05266041433185063 where smaller members of its family are near the upper score limit. Extending a different diene-containing linker gives 8.672801865236684e-07, while tiny fragments, long polyethers and very large polar or polyaryl structures occupy low tails. One complete set contains 191 of 870 proposals above 50 heavy atoms versus 128 Parent proposals. Other sets have lower median or upper-tail size than their Parent, so this is context-dependent rather than evidence for a universal size limit.
transferable_gaps.gap: Size-changing proposals can lose the useful connected arrangement through over-elaboration or excessive fragmentation.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Provide growth, contraction and linker alternatives that preserve a coherent accepted core and its useful local donor, acceptor, amine and aromatic relationships. Let feedback determine tolerated complexity instead of relying on whole-motif duplication or removing the molecular framework entirely.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Nonchiral Murcko scaffold counts are 612, 689, 599, 720 and 564 across the child sets. Yet their high excerpts repeatedly decorate short carbonyl/aza-aromatic linkers, contracted hydrazone/carbonyl cores, arylpiperazine/oxygen-ring families, dense nitrogen/carbonyl assemblies and N-fluorinated sulfur or carbonyl families. Different seeds access other chemistry, but new graph identity often reflects a local ring change or peripheral elaboration rather than a well-supported distinct useful core.
transferable_gaps.gap: Useful core coverage remains uneven despite broad generation of distinct molecular graphs.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Maintain multiple accepted chemical families and enable core replacements that preserve useful spatial and electronic relationships among their functional groups. Assess core chemistry and attachment context rather than counting a changed string, extra ring closure or peripheral substituent as sufficient useful diversity.

method_name: Genetic GFN: reciprocal learning between a flow policy and graph search
method_thesis: Anchor the root in Genetic GFN: alternately generate molecules with a GFlowNet policy, refine the resulting scored population through graph crossover and mutation, and distill scored descendants back into the policy using rank-weighted off-policy replay. The policy uses trajectory balance with a learned log normalizer and regularization toward a frozen prior. [Kim et al., Section 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.05961v4) describe this mechanism. Train the prior only on the permitted unlabeled corpus. Each objective starts with clean policy adaptation, replay and population state initialized from its supplied observations. Use a positive terminal reward increasing with the observed maximization score. Schedule policy and genetic phases around the evaluator's announced feedback; both produce new molecules, and all reward-bearing training records come from accepted observations. Later policy samples must enter genetic populations, and accepted graph descendants must affect subsequent policy updates. Generate further valid, canonical-unique structures to fill announced batches, without corpus ranking or a fixed molecular library. The hypothesis is that learned global proposals propagate local discoveries into new promising regions and then support further graph refinement, raising the mean of five independent final Top-1 scores. Published larger-budget gains do not establish that this reciprocal learning becomes useful quickly enough here.

activation_observables.measurement: Per preparation seed, verify the registered EMA recurrence, update count and decay through source, bounded logged coordinate probes and raw/EMA parameter identities at validation boundaries. Report nonzero raw-to-EMA parameter distance and differing likelihoods on the identical holdout; a counter alone or an EMA name on raw weights is insufficient. Reconstruct EMA checkpoint selection by minimum ordinary holdout NLL and earliest-step tie-breaking, independently of the raw-NLL tracker that controls stopping. Report raw and EMA losses over validation time, initial NLL, selected EMA loss/step, raw minimum loss/step and completed training updates. Compare raw minimum weights with preserved Parent checkpoint identities when available to establish whether the raw trajectory was retained. Better EMA loss would support the stabilizing-weight hypothesis; worse loss is negative representation evidence despite a correct averaging recurrence. Finite coordinate audits do not claim independent reconstruction of every full parameter tensor at every update.
activation_observables.name: unlabeled_holdout_likelihood_change

activation_observables.measurement: Independently classify the complete final diagnostic raw strings from the selected EMA and ordinary raw-minimum priors with the unchanged molecular checks. Verify panel count equals that preparation's holdout row count, chunk size equals its inherited training minibatch size, and the same private purpose/chunk streams were used for both models without selection feedback. Report paired valid-terminated and canonical-unique yields, duplicates, invalids and missing EOS by seed and pooled. A positive independent yield difference supports useful generative transfer; a zero or negative difference is negative downstream evidence, not failure to average weights. Separately report existing adapted-policy raw outcomes and molecular findings, distinguishing first neural batches from later graph feedback. Pure-prior diagnostics, adapted-policy validity and final oracle scores are different measurements and must not be substituted for one another.

activation_observables.measurement: Verify exact raw model restoration and unchanged parameter identities around EMA validation, with original row draws, gradient formula, optimizer/scaler state semantics and raw-NLL stopping intact. Check that the published tensor state and recorded selected step match the selected EMA receipt, and that reload verification succeeds. finding_summary.headline: Averaged priors improved holdout loss and pure-prior yield, with a small, uneven score gain.
finding_summary.insights:
This provides evidence that averaging the same unlabeled weight trajectory can produce a better reusable prior without changing training examples, gradient updates or the online algorithm. Exact raw checkpoint identities and matching raw loss histories rule out altered raw training as the explanation. The final pure-prior comparison was excluded from checkpoint selection, so its consistent yield improvement adds evidence beyond the heldout criterion that selected the average. The early lag also limits the result: the benefit appears after substantial training, and is not evidence that averaged weights are preferable throughout learning.

Better pure-prior likelihood and parseable yield were insufficient to improve validity after task adaptation or provide broad task gains. The chemistry explains why the score increase deserves a narrower interpretation: ordinary aryl/carbonyl and amine families coexist with N-fluorinated motifs, unusual hydrogen-bearing sulfur, azide/acyl-halide assemblies and contracted rings. Favorable scores do not establish those connections as necessary or synthetically credible. Explicit stereochemical configurations remain absent. The remaining question is how much of the improved reusable prior can survive accepted-score adaptation while retaining credible functional-group attachment and useful core coverage; this experiment demonstrates the averaging effect, but does not resolve that downstream limitation.
finding_summary.results:
The averaged weights were distinct from the raw weights throughout validation, and all 6,633 logged coordinate updates matched the registered recurrence. The raw training losses and final raw checkpoint identities remained exactly equal to the Parent. All three preparations completed 29,742 updates and selected the final averaged state by ordinary holdout loss. Mean selected token loss fell from 0.564577 to 0.559834, improving in every seed. Averaging initially lagged the raw model, but its loss stayed lower at every validation from step 5,000 onward in all three seeds.

The final unscored diagnostic also improved in every seed. Across three 4,096-sample panels per model, valid terminated yield increased from 90.41% to 91.85%, giving 177 more valid strings. Each individual panel had no canonical duplicates or missing EOS, so its valid and canonical-unique yields were equal. The gains were 2.34, 1.54 and 0.44 percentage points across seeds. This pure-prior gain did not carry through to higher adapted-policy validity: across the same 12,000 online draws, validity was 70.06% versus Parent 70.34%, with first-batch validity 90.92% versus 91.17% and later-batch validity 67.74% versus 68.03%.

All fifteen tasks completed. Three-seed mean final Top-1 rose from 0.520669 to 0.527370; paired gains were 0.000602, 0.004046 and 0.015453. The improvement was concentrated in sitagliptin, while deco-hop and median scores fell in every seed and zaleplon was mixed. Recorded mean preparation time was 238.0 seconds versus 259.5 seconds, with identical training horizons; these total timings do not isolate the extra averaging and diagnostic cost.

finding_summary.headline: Averaged priors improved holdout loss and pure-prior yield, with a small, uneven score gain.
finding_summary.insights:
This provides evidence that averaging the same unlabeled weight trajectory can produce a better reusable prior without changing training examples, gradient updates or the online algorithm. Exact raw checkpoint identities and matching raw loss histories rule out altered raw training as the explanation. The final pure-prior comparison was excluded from checkpoint selection, so its consistent yield improvement adds evidence beyond the heldout criterion that selected the average. The early lag also limits the result: the benefit appears after substantial training, and is not evidence that averaged weights are preferable throughout learning.

Better pure-prior likelihood and parseable yield were insufficient to improve validity after task adaptation or provide broad task gains. The chemistry explains why the score increase deserves a narrower interpretation: ordinary aryl/carbonyl and amine families coexist with N-fluorinated motifs, unusual hydrogen-bearing sulfur, azide/acyl-halide assemblies and contracted rings. Favorable scores do not establish those connections as necessary or synthetically credible. Explicit stereochemical configurations remain absent. The remaining question is how much of the improved reusable prior can survive accepted-score adaptation while retaining credible functional-group attachment and useful core coverage; this experiment demonstrates the averaging effect, but does not resolve that downstream limitation.
finding_summary.results:
The averaged weights were distinct from the raw weights throughout validation, and all 6,633 logged coordinate updates matched the registered recurrence. The raw training losses and final raw checkpoint identities remained exactly equal to the Parent. All three preparations completed 29,742 updates and selected the final averaged state by ordinary holdout loss. Mean selected token loss fell from 0.564577 to 0.559834, improving in every seed. Averaging initially lagged the raw model, but its loss stayed lower at every validation from step 5,000 onward in all three seeds.

The final unscored diagnostic also improved in every seed. Across three 4,096-sample panels per model, valid terminated yield increased from 90.41% to 91.85%, giving 177 more valid strings. Each individual panel had no canonical duplicates or missing EOS, so its valid and canonical-unique yields were equal. The gains were 2.34, 1.54 and 0.44 percentage points across seeds. This pure-prior gain did not carry through to higher adapted-policy validity: across the same 12,000 online draws, validity was 70.06% versus Parent 70.34%, with first-batch validity 90.92% versus 91.17% and later-batch validity 67.74% versus 68.03%.

All fifteen tasks completed. Three-seed mean final Top-1 rose from 0.520669 to 0.527370; paired gains were 0.000602, 0.004046 and 0.015453. The improvement was concentrated in sitagliptin, while deco-hop and median scores fell in every seed and zaleplon was mixed. Recorded mean preparation time was 238.0 seconds versus 259.5 seconds, with identical training horizons; these total timings do not isolate the extra averaging and diagnostic cost.

finding_summary.headline: Averaged priors improved holdout loss and pure-prior yield, with a small, uneven score gain.
finding_summary.insights:
This provides evidence that averaging the same unlabeled weight trajectory can produce a better reusable prior without changing training examples, gradient updates or the online algorithm. Exact raw checkpoint identities and matching raw loss histories rule out altered raw training as the explanation. The final pure-prior comparison was excluded from checkpoint selection, so its consistent yield improvement adds evidence beyond the heldout criterion that selected the average. The early lag also limits the result: the benefit appears after substantial training, and is not evidence that averaged weights are preferable throughout learning.

Better pure-prior likelihood and parseable yield were insufficient to improve validity after task adaptation or provide broad task gains. The chemistry explains why the score increase deserves a narrower interpretation: ordinary aryl/carbonyl and amine families coexist with N-fluorinated motifs, unusual hydrogen-bearing sulfur, azide/acyl-halide assemblies and contracted rings. Favorable scores do not establish those connections as necessary or synthetically credible. Explicit stereochemical configurations remain absent. The remaining question is how much of the improved reusable prior can survive accepted-score adaptation while retaining credible functional-group attachment and useful core coverage; this experiment demonstrates the averaging effect, but does not resolve that downstream limitation.
finding_summary.results:
The averaged weights were distinct from the raw weights throughout validation, and all 6,633 logged coordinate updates matched the registered recurrence. The raw training losses and final raw checkpoint identities remained exactly equal to the Parent. All three preparations completed 29,742 updates and selected the final averaged state by ordinary holdout loss. Mean selected token loss fell from 0.564577 to 0.559834, improving in every seed. Averaging initially lagged the raw model, but its loss stayed lower at every validation from step 5,000 onward in all three seeds.

The final unscored diagnostic also improved in every seed. Across three 4,096-sample panels per model, valid terminated yield increased from 90.41% to 91.85%, giving 177 more valid strings. Each individual panel had no canonical duplicates or missing EOS, so its valid and canonical-unique yields were equal. The gains were 2.34, 1.54 and 0.44 percentage points across seeds. This pure-prior gain did not carry through to higher adapted-policy validity: across the same 12,000 online draws, validity was 70.06% versus Parent 70.34%, with first-batch validity 90.92% versus 91.17% and later-batch validity 67.74% versus 68.03%.

All fifteen tasks completed. Three-seed mean final Top-1 rose from 0.520669 to 0.527370; paired gains were 0.000602, 0.004046 and 0.015453. The improvement was concentrated in sitagliptin, while deco-hop and median scores fell in every seed and zaleplon was mixed. Recorded mean preparation time was 238.0 seconds versus 259.5 seconds, with identical training horizons; these total timings do not isolate the extra averaging and diagnostic cost.

molecular_assessment.headline: Aryl carbonyl and amine families coexist with azide/acyl-halide assemblies, N-fluorinated rings and unusual hydrogen-bearing sulfur.
molecular_assessment.overall_character: All 4,500 child and 4,500 Parent trajectory rows were read. Each node supplies 900 observations per task, including 870 optimizer proposals, for 4,350 proposals overall. Every emitted child SMILES parses with the supplied RDKit environment. The output contains ordinary aryl ketones and amides, aza-aromatics, arylpiperazines and oxygen-containing rings, but also contracted unsaturated rings, complex nitrogen/carbonyl assemblies, hydrazones, azides, acyl halides and N-fluorinated structures. The digest ring-closure rates are 0.9759–0.9920 and aromatic-marker rates 0.9241–0.9770; these measure presence in SMILES text rather than aromatic atom fraction or geometric plausibility. Read-only RDKit median heavy-atom counts are 25, 36, 30, 33 and 26 in the supplied task order, with median ring counts of three, four, four, five and three. Chemical plausibility is mixed: several leading families have conventional ingredients, while other high examples contain sensitive bonding and unusual valence or ring topology. Each task has stereocentre_rate 0.0; unassigned stereogenic centres occur in 325, 312, 540, 519 and 367 optimizer proposals respectively, and assigned centres in none. Different seeds reach different families, but their high neighborhoods often concentrate on related decorations or ring edits. These observations describe the chemistry and its limitations without judging mechanism activation or node eligibility.

per_task.generated_character: The leading seed-2 family joins a hydroxyquinazoline-like bicyclic aza-aromatic group to an ortho-methylphenyl carbonyl group through a short substituted linker. The leader is a ketone with a methyl-bearing stereogenic carbon; it has 24 heavy atoms and three aromatic six-membered rings. A close family contains the corresponding tertiary benzamide connection. Other high molecules use a diaryl ether with sulfinamide or thioamide linkage, and seed 0 explores aryl thioethers/carboxylic acids connected to thiazole-like or contracted four-membered unsaturated nitrogen rings. Much of this is recognizable carbonyl and heteroaromatic chemistry, although the short unsaturated ring and some sulfur attachments are less straightforward. The child and Parent both have median 25 heavy atoms and three rings. Parent leaders included biaryl pyrazole/acetanilide and quinoline/urea arrangements, so the change is in useful attachment patterns rather than a general new ability to make aromatic or carbonyl groups.
liabilities: A high seed-0 example contains a four-membered unsaturated nitrogen ring. Its valence-valid graph does not establish low strain or synthetic accessibility.
Sulfinamide, thioamide, sulfonamide and thioether attachments have different electronic and reactive behavior; the score does not make them interchangeable or establish their stability.
Tiny fragments and much larger linked structures occur in the low tail, while the useful examples are moderate in size. Their substituted and bridged centres are not stereochemically specified.
missing_features: Chemically distinct compact cores preserving the useful carbonyl, aza-aromatic and linker relationships are not consistently established among the high neighbors; many modifications instead alter several local relationships at once.

approach.method_basis: The Parent trains a recurrent SMILES model on original unlabeled molecular strings and publishes the single checkpoint with the best ordinary heldout token loss. An objective starts an adaptable copy and retains the published model as a frozen reference. Accepted neural samples refresh a graph-breeding population and provide a protected parent at the first graph handoff; a fingerprint posterior using accepted scores selects the other offspring. Graph observations then train the neural policy through trajectory balance and the learned normalizer. That complete reciprocal method is retained. Only the estimate of reusable neural weights produced by unlabeled preparation changes.
approach.novelty: Track an exponential moving average of the unlabeled training weights and let ordinary heldout token loss select among those averaged checkpoints. The average combines nearby stages of the same training trajectory, rather than publishing one instantaneous state. This differs from the tested alternative-string augmentation and molecular-yield checkpoint ranking, and from changing the frequency of training examples. Original data, gradient updates and online adaptation stay fixed, while a final unlabeled comparison measures what the averaged and ordinary minimum-loss priors emit.
